hops.title: Say it: a teaspoon of soil is full of tiny helpers
hops.text: Right after you spoon soil into the tubs, when the dirt looks empty to your child, try saying, "A spoonful of garden soil can hold hundreds of millions of tiny living things, too small to see." Add that some of them, bacteria and fungi, can help rot the apple and bread, along with tiny mold spores already on the food.

sources.citation: Ohio State University Extension, Role of Soil Bacteria (ANR-36)
University of Minnesota Department of Soil, Water, and Climate, Healthy Soil, Healthy Plants

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A parent and child seen from behind leaning over a wooden table to look at a teaspoon full of dark soil.
image.caption: A teaspoon of healthy garden soil can hold hundreds of millions of bacteria, too small to see.

hops.title: Point at it: pill bugs under damp leaves
hops.text: Outdoors with your child, lift a damp fallen leaf, leaving anything that might sting or bite alone. Spot a pill bug? Wait for it to uncurl, then count its legs together. Grown-ups have seven pairs. These harmless crab cousins eat mostly rotting plant bits. They breathe air with tiny lung-like parts, and damp places keep them from drying out.

sources.citation: Purdue Extension Entomology, Distinguishing Insects from Their Relatives
University of Kentucky Department of Entomology, ENTFACT-439: Sowbugs and Pillbugs
Shultz JW (2018), A guide to the identification of the terrestrial Isopoda of Maryland, U.S.A. (Crustacea), ZooKeys 801: 207-228
Franklin, Byron and Gillett-Kaufman, Pillbug, Roly-Poly, Woodlouse Armadillidium vulgare (EENY630), UF/IFAS EDIS

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Close-up of two small gray pill bugs on damp soil beneath a lifted autumn leaf, one walking and one curled into a ball.
image.caption: Pill bugs are harmless crab cousins that hide in damp leaves and munch dead plant bits.

hops.title: Compare it: mold eats like a kitchen sponge
hops.text: Hold up a dry kitchen sponge. You put food inside your belly to digest it, but mold does it the other way around. Like other fungi, it pours digestive juices straight onto the bread, breaking the food down outside its body. Then it soaks up the tiny bits through its surface, the way the sponge soaks up water.

sources.citation: OpenStax Biology 2e, Section 24.1 Characteristics of Fungi

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A yellow kitchen sponge resting on a sunlit kitchen counter and soaking up a small puddle of water.
image.caption: Fungi break down food outside their bodies first, then soak up nutrients like a sponge.
